summary: Surveys deployed and experimental in-network storage systems and discusses how they apply to the DECADE architecture, which separates application data storage from the applications themselves. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reviews the storage systems that sit inside a network and serve content to applications, then checks which of them could support the DECADE design. DECADE wants applications to control what they have stored in the network and how much of the network's capacity they use. The survey finds that none of the systems reviewed can do all of that.

subtitle: A review of storage systems that live inside the network, and what each one still cannot do for peer-to-peer applications.

tldr.problem: Content distribution puts heavy load on network infrastructure, and existing caches give the application no say over the storage it uses or the bandwidth it consumes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys deployed and experimental in-network storage systems against a common seven-component model, then checks those systems and the related storage protocols against the requirements of the DECADE architecture.
tldr.outcome: No surveyed system or protocol fully meets the DECADE requirements. The survey points to a standard protocol that would let peer-to-peer applications access and control in-network storage.

facts.label: Storage capacity per price
facts.value: At least a 30-fold increase over the last two decades

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6392 surveys deployed and experimental in-network storage systems and describes their applicability for the DECADE (DECoupled Application Data Enroute) architecture. DECADE is an architecture that gives applications access to provider-based in-network storage for content distribution, so that content distribution applications can place less load on network infrastructure. The example given is a peer of a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) application that uploads to other peers through its in-network storage, saving its use of last-mile uplink bandwidth.

The stated motivation is the substantial increase in capacity and reduction in cost of storage systems: over the last two decades there has been at least a 30-fold increase in the amount of storage a customer can get for a given price, for flash memory and for hard disk drives.

DECADE differs from existing content caches, whose control fully resides with the owners of the caching devices, because DECADE also allows applications to control access to their allocated in-network storage and the resources consumed while accessing that storage, which the RFC names as bandwidth, connections and storage space. The document is not meant to point out shortcomings of existing solutions, but to indicate where capabilities required by DECADE are not provided by existing systems.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC reviews the storage systems that sit inside a network and serve content to applications, and asks which of them could support the DECADE design. DECADE wants applications to control what they have stored in the network and how much of the network's capacity they use.

sections.title: The Components of an In-Network Storage System
sections.content:
Before surveying individual technologies, the RFC sets out a common model, so that every system is evaluated the same way. It compares systems on seven components. The Data Access Interface is the set of operations available for accessing data; solutions typically allow both read and write operations, though the mechanisms differ. Data Management Operations are operations such as delete and move, provided to users rather than to system administrators. Data Search Capability is the ability to search or enumerate stored content, for example finding the items a given user stored over a given period of time.

Access Control Authorization has three types. Public-unrestricted content is widely available to all clients, like reading Wikipedia on the Web or using an anonymous FTP site. Public-restricted content is available to a restricted but still potentially large set of clients without any confidential credentials, like a television episode that can only be viewed in selected countries or networks. Private content is made available only to clients presenting the required confidential credentials, such as a password or key. A scenario may combine types: the read of content may be public-unrestricted while the write to the same system is private.

The Resource Control Interface is how users manage the resources on the storage system that can be used by other peers, such as bandwidth or connections, and the system may let a user state a time for which the resources are granted. The Discovery Mechanism is how users find the location of the in-network storage, the access interface, the resource control interface or other interfaces. The Storage Mode describes how data is structured inside the system: a file system organises files into a hierarchical tree of directories and files; object-based storage keeps discrete chunks of data with no predefined hierarchy or meta-structure; block-based storage keeps a raw sequence of bytes that a client reads and writes at offsets. Storage mode is about the internal structure and need not match how a client accesses the data, so a caching system may cache objects with hierarchical names while internally using object-based storage.
sections.plainLanguage: To compare the systems fairly, the RFC scores each one against the same seven questions: how data is read and written, whether users can delete or move it, whether it can be searched, who is allowed in, whether users can cap the bandwidth and connections they consume, how the storage is found, and how the data is organised inside the system.

sections.title: The Systems the Survey Covers
sections.content:
Section 4 surveys in-network storage systems using the model above. It covers systems that are widely deployed today, systems that are just being deployed, and experimental systems, and it covers both traditional client-server architectures and P2P architectures. The systems are listed alphabetically and each one gets a note on its relevance to DECADE. The fourteen surveyed systems are Amazon S3, BranchCache, Cache-and-Forward Architecture, Cloud Data Management Interface, Content Delivery Network, Delay-Tolerant Network, Named Data Networking, Network of Information, Network Traffic Redundancy Elimination, OceanStore, P2P Cache, Photo Sharing, Usenet and Web Cache.

Three of them show how far apart these systems are. Amazon S3 provides an online storage service over Web interfaces where users create buckets and store objects. It supports reading and writing objects, deleting stored objects, listing the contents of buckets to find objects matching criteria, all three access control types, and discovery through a well-known DNS name. It provides no resource control interface, and the simplifications it made for scalability include the absence of a general hierarchical namespace and the inability to update the contents of existing data.

A Content Delivery Network (CDN) distributes content to cache or edge servers located close to users. It has four parts: content delivery, request routing, distribution and accounting. Clients usually get only read access, and writing is typically a private operation for the content provider. A Web cache, widely deployed by many ISPs since the late 1990s, stores copies of documents between the server and the client so that later requests can be served from the cache. Users read from it explicitly but cannot write into it, the access control method for clients is public-unrestricted, and content that is authenticated or encrypted, or flagged private at the HTTP level by the origin server, is not cached at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey covers fourteen systems, from widely deployed services to research prototypes. They differ in the basics: who may write, whether a user can search what is stored, and whether the user can limit how much of the network the stored data may use.

sections.title: Storage and Related Protocols
sections.content:
Section 5 surveys existing storage and other related protocols and comments on how well they fit the DECADE use cases. The protocols are listed alphabetically: HTTP, iSCSI, NFS, OAuth and WebDAV.

HTTP is the key protocol of the World Wide Web. It is a stateless client-server protocol that allows applications to be designed using the REST model, and it supports uploading as well as downloading. HTTP is used by several of the in-network storage systems surveyed earlier, including CDNs, photo sharing and Web cache. Using HTTP as the underlying protocol of a storage system means no extra software is needed in the client, because every standard Web browser is built on HTTP. It supports read and write through the GET, PUT and POST methods and all three access control types, and clients typically address HTTP servers by a hostname resolved with DNS. It does not provide data management operations, a data search capability or a resource control interface.

The RFC's conclusion on the protocols is that all of them were primarily designed for client-server architectures and not for P2P, although some could conceivably be adapted. The majority do not support low-latency access for applications such as live streaming, which was one of the key general requirements for DECADE, and the majority do not support any form of resource control interface, which is also a key DECADE capability. Nearly all of them do support reading and writing content, some form of access control, some form of error indication, and the ability to traverse firewalls and NATs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also reviews the protocols those systems speak, including HTTP. Most were built for a client and a server rather than for peers, most cannot serve live streams with low delay, and most give the user no way to cap the bandwidth or connections the stored data uses. Nearly all of them can read and write content, check who is asking, report errors and get through firewalls.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Many in-network storage systems have been successful, but they were designed for use cases different from the ones DECADE defines. Most of the surveyed in-network storage systems and protocols were designed for client-server architectures and not P2P. The RFC states plainly that no surveyed system or protocol has the functionality and features to fully meet the set of requirements defined for DECADE.

DECADE aims to provide a standard protocol allowing P2P applications, including content providers, to make use of in-network storage to reduce the traffic burden on ISP networks, while enabling those applications to control access to content they have placed in in-network storage. Defining a standard protocol can also reduce the complexity of in-network storage, because multiple P2P application protocols no longer need to be implemented by in-network storage systems.

The survey is representative rather than exhaustive. Rather than enumerating every system, the authors chose some typical techniques that lead to derivative works.
sections.plainLanguage: The conclusion is that none of the systems reviewed does everything DECADE needs. The value of a standard protocol would be that applications get control over their stored content, and storage systems stop having to implement every peer-to-peer application separately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document is a survey of existing in-network storage systems, and introduces no security considerations beyond those of the surveyed systems. For more information on the security considerations of DECADE, the RFC points to the DECADE Problem Statement.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not add security rules of its own. It says the security questions belong to the systems it surveyed and to the DECADE problem statement.
